porous_phi60.name: Flow Through Porous Rock
porous_phi60.question: How readily does a grain pack transmit fluid, and why?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: How readily does a grain pack transmit fluid, and why?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: A force drives fluid through the connected gaps between solid grains. Narrow passages restrict the flow while wider channels carry more; once settled, the permeability k describes how readily the sample transmits fluid.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Keep the porosity and change the seed (Same Porosity, Different Connectivity scene) — k changes because the pores connect differently.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The permeability readout k = ν U_D/g, with U_D the flow averaged over the whole sample.
more: Sweep the porosity from 0.45 to 0.8 with the sweep tool.
Sweep the driving strength: in the Darcy regime k must not depend on it.

layers.title: Physical explanation
layers.text:
Soils, rocks, filters, catalyst beds, even bone — all are porous: solid matrices threaded by pore space. When you drive fluid through, it cannot go straight; it winds through the connected pores, speeding up in the throats and stalling in the dead ends. Henry Darcy discovered in 1856, while engineering Dijon's water supply, that despite this complexity the average flow rate is simply proportional to the pressure gradient. The proportionality constant — the permeability k — packs all the pore geometry into one number with units of area.

Permeability is what petroleum engineers need to predict oil recovery, what hydrologists need for groundwater, and what battery and fuel-cell designers tune in porous electrodes. You cannot read k off a photo of the pores; you have to solve the flow. 'Digital rock physics' does exactly that — simulate the pore-scale flow in a 3D/2D image of the material and measure the averaged response. That is precisely what this exhibit does with lattice-Boltzmann.

Here a constant body force drives flow through a random grain pack in a periodic box; once steady, the volume-averaged velocity ⟨u⟩ gives k = ν⟨u⟩/g. Drop the porosity and the tortuous paths choke down — permeability falls steeply, as the Kozeny–Carman relation predicts.

layers.title: Equations, symbols and assumptions
layers.text:
• ⟨u⟩ — the velocity averaged over the whole sample (Darcy/superficial velocity)
• k — permeability: the area-dimensioned measure of how easily fluid passes
• μ = ρν — dynamic viscosity; ∇p — the driving pressure gradient (here a body force)
• φ — porosity, the void fraction; k climbs steeply with φ
• Kozeny–Carman: k ≈ φ³d²/[180(1−φ)²] links k to porosity and grain size d

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: Fluid at rest inside a random grain pack (equilibrium populations at zero velocity), then accelerated by the body force; the permeability is read from the final state.
layers.bc: Periodic in x and y with a constant body force along x or y; no-slip bounce-back on every grain surface.

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: The same D2Q9 lattice-Boltzmann scheme, here in a periodic box driven by a constant body force (Guo forcing) through a random grain pack, in the viscous (Stokes) regime, along x or y. Permeability is k = ν U_D/g with U_D the superficial velocity (flow averaged over the whole sample, solids counting as zero) and g the body force per unit mass; the pore-average velocity U_D/φ is reported separately.
layers.checks: Numerical check: the same solver reproduces the analytical plane-Poiseuille permeability (tests/, error 0.07 %). The Kozeny–Carman line in the plot is an empirical 3-D relation shown for orientation only; agreement with it is not claimed for this 2-D geometry.

layers.title: References
items: Bear, J. (1972). Dynamics of Fluids in Porous Media. Elsevier (Darcy's law, Kozeny–Carman).
Guo, Z., Zheng, C. & Shi, B. (2002). Discrete lattice effects on the forcing term in the lattice Boltzmann method. Phys. Rev. E 65, 046308.
Krüger, T. et al. (2017). The Lattice Boltzmann Method: Principles and Practice. Springer.

porous_connectivity.name: Similar Porosity, Different Arrangement
porous_connectivity.question: Why can equal porosity produce different permeability?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: Why can equal porosity produce different permeability?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: The same target porosity and grain size as the default sample, but a different random arrangement. The measured porosities differ slightly (about 0.598 versus 0.600 at Medium — the random pack does not hit the target exactly; both are shown in the readouts); the paths through the pore space differ much more.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Compare k with the porous_phi60 scene (run history → Compare).

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The streamline view: a few wide channels carry most of the flow.
more: Try seeds 2–10 with the sweep tool to see the spread of k at fixed porosity.

porous_aniso.name: Directional Permeability
porous_aniso.question: Does the sample conduct flow equally in different directions?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: Does the sample conduct flow equally in different directions?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: The same grain pack driven along y instead of x. The permeability tensor of a random pack is nearly isotropic; an arranged or elongated pack is not.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Run with direction x and y on the same seed and compare k_x with k_y.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: k_y versus k_x in the run history.
more: Lower the porosity to 0.45: anisotropy of the random pack grows as fewer paths remain.

porosity.label: Porosity  φ
porosity.help: Fraction of the sample that is open pore space. Lower porosity (denser grain packing) → far lower permeability.

grain.label: Grain size
grain.help: Radius of the packed grains as a fraction of the sample height.

seed.label: Random seed
seed.help: Seed of the random grain arrangement: change it to compare samples with the same porosity but different connectivity.

direction.label: Driving direction
direction.help: Direction of the body force. Run both to measure the directional permeability k_x and k_y of the same sample (anisotropy).

strength.label: Driving strength
strength.help: Multiplier on the body force (1 = 1.2e-5 lattice units). In the Darcy regime k must not depend on it — sweep it to check linearity.

resolution.label: Resolution
resolution.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

duration.label: Duration (×)
